cultivar: Chinary seedling bushes and clonals (AV2, B157, P312); the muscatel note is most reliable on older Chinary bushes
processing: Full wither, orthodox rolling and much fuller oxidation than the first flush (close to a conventional black tea), then firing; the larger summer leaf gives a darker, rounder cup.
harvest_season: Late May through June, between the spring pluck and the monsoon; mid-June lots are often the most muscatel.
appearance_dry: Well-twisted brown-black leaf with plenty of golden tips and a few lighter olive strands.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber to coppery orange, clear.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf with some greenish patches, larger than first-flush leaf.
taste_profile: Ripe muscat grape and dried apricot over a rounder, honeyed body, with moderate tannin and a long, slightly woody finish.

brewing.notes: Water just under the boil, 3–4 minutes. It takes a drop of milk better than the first flush, but the fruit shows best plain.

vintage_note: Sold as 'Second Flush' with the harvest year and the estate (and often a grade such as FTGFOP1 and an invoice number); the best lots are marketed from July onward. Second flush keeps better than first flush because it is more oxidised: a sealed pack is good for 1–2 years and some drinkers prefer it after a few months of rest. 'Muscatel' on a label is a tasting claim, not a grade; only some lots in a good year really show it, so taste before buying a large bag.
description:
Darjeeling second flush is the early-summer harvest, picked from late May into June once the bushes have recovered from the spring pluck and before the monsoon arrives. If the first flush is Darjeeling at its brightest, the second flush is Darjeeling at its ripest: fuller, darker and famous for the 'muscatel' note of sweet muscat grape that nothing else quite reproduces.

The summer leaf is larger and tougher, so it is withered and oxidised far more fully than the spring leaf and comes out looking like a conventional black tea, brown with golden tips. The muscatel character is widely credited to tiny green leafhoppers (jassids) nibbling the leaf, which pushes the plant to produce aromatic compounds that oxidation then turns into that grapey, honeyed note; the same mechanism is behind Taiwan's Oriental Beauty. Not every lot gets it, and makers prize the ones that do.

In the cup look for muscat grape, dried apricot and a honeyed, rounder body with moderate tannin and a long, slightly woody finish. It is more forgiving than the first flush: water just under the boil, three to four minutes, and a second steep. It can take a drop of milk, but you will lose the fruit; try it plain first.

Labels read 'Second Flush' plus the year and the estate, usually with a grade such as FTGFOP1 and sometimes an invoice number. The word 'muscatel' is a tasting claim rather than a grade, and in a poor year even a famous garden may not show it strongly, so buy a sample before a big bag. Castleton, Jungpana, Margaret's Hope, Thurbo and Goomtee second flushes are the classic references.

Because it is more oxidised, second flush keeps better than first flush; a sealed pack is fine for a year or two, and some drinkers prefer it after a few months of rest. It is also the Darjeeling that pairs best with food, from scones to a mild cheese.
